device.name: Lutron Caseta Smart Bridge 2
device.notes:
Lutron Caseta Smart Bridge 2 advertises multiple local services. LEAP on port 8081 is the modern local control protocol: newline-delimited JSON over a direct mutual-TLS socket. LAP on port 8083 is deprecated for control but is still where certificate pairing happens. The _lutron._tcp record exposes stable bridge identity including MACADDR, firmware CODEVER, system type, and device class; its SRV port 22 is the bridge's SSH, not LEAP. HomeKit HAP is separately advertised on port 4548.
This is the non-Pro bridge (L-BDG2): LEAP only, no LIP/Telnet integration. The Smart Bridge PRO (L-BDGPRO2) adds Lutron Integration Protocol on Telnet 23 with its own integration IDs, which this spec does not document. The bridge talks to Caseta dimmers, switches, shades and Picos over Clear Connect Type A (431-437 MHz in North America), not Zigbee, Z-Wave or Wi-Fi; a Pico paired directly to a dimmer keeps working without the bridge, which is needed for the app, schedules, remote access and third-party integration. Community teardowns describe a TI AM335x Linux host with an STM32 coprocessor driving the sub-GHz radio (reported, not a vendor BOM).
This project does NOT drive LEAP yet, so the bridge is classified integration: identify_only — the app recognises it from its _leap._tcp / _lutron._tcp advertisements and hands the user off to Lutron's own app rather than claiming control. The full LEAP handshake, certificate pairing and command surface below are documented and kept intact for when a LEAP transport is implemented; nothing here has been removed. There is no local web admin UI to deep-link to (control is the LEAP protocol itself), so no admin_url is set.

procedures.basis: The pairing flow implemented by the open LEAP clients this spec follows (pylutron-caseta 0.30.1, which Home Assistant uses). Not replayed against a bridge here; this project's probe reached only the 8083 certificate gate.
procedures.name: Hold the button on the back of the bridge while submitting the CSR

steps.action: Generate an RSA or EC key pair and a certificate signing request on the client.
Connect to port 8083 over TLS with the initial LAP client certificate.
Press and hold the button on the back of the bridge.
Wait for a status message listing PhysicalAccess in Body.Status.Permissions, then submit the CSR.
steps.expect: A signed client certificate and the bridge CA in the response.

exclusivity.recovery: Nothing to clear before pairing: the bridge signs a certificate for each client that asks, so a new controller does not displace an existing one.

pairing.notes: Unusually for this repository, the credential is a client certificate rather than a token, and the pairing is where the trust in both directions is established at once: the bridge learns the client's public key, and the client learns the CA it will pin. Losing the private key means holding the button again; there is no way to re-download it.

pin.notes: Not a code but a certificate: the client generates its own key pair and CSR, and the bridge signs it during the button hold. What the client stores afterwards is its signed certificate, its private key and the bridge's CA — the last of which it pins for every later LEAP session.

issued_to_client: Client certificate and private key signed by the bridge CA
credentials.notes: This is the strongest local auth model of any device documented here: no shared secret, no cloud, and a client credential that can be revoked by resetting the bridge.

factory_reset.effect: Network reset only: drops network settings and external integrations (including issued client certificates). Per Lutron documentation this does NOT delete previously paired devices, scenes or schedules; no button procedure wipes the associated-device list.

procedures.indicator: Release the button once the light ring begins to blink.
procedures.name: Rear button held 20s (network reset)

steps.action: Press and hold the small black button on the back of the bridge for 20 seconds; release when the light ring begins to blink.
steps.notes: Vendor-documented network reset; paired devices, scenes and schedules survive. A 40-second hold (LED flashes again at 40s) performs a HomeKit reset.

methods.description: The bridge is Ethernet-only, so there is no wireless provisioning; what needs documenting is the LEAP pairing that follows, because unlike most devices here the bridge issues the client a real X.509 certificate and refuses anonymous connections afterwards.
methods.name: Ethernet, then button-held CSR signing

stages.description: Ethernet to the router; the bridge takes a DHCP lease and advertises _lutron._tcp.local.
stages.name: Get the bridge onto the LAN

steps.action: Connect the bridge with Ethernet and apply power.

stages.description: The client generates a key pair and CSR, opens the pairing channel, and waits for the bridge to report that its physical button is being held; only then does it submit the CSR. The bridge signs it and returns the client certificate plus its own CA certificate, which the client pins for all later LEAP sessions.
stages.name: Sign the client's CSR at the bridge button

steps.action: Generate an RSA/EC key pair and a certificate signing request on the client.
Open a TLS connection to port 8083 presenting the initial LAP client certificate that open LEAP clients ship (public, not reproduced here).
steps.expect: The handshake completes; without a client certificate the bridge aborts it with a bad-certificate alert.

steps.action: Press and hold the button on the back of the bridge.
Wait for the bridge's unsolicited status message granting physical access.
steps.expect: A JSON line whose Header.ContentType begins 'status;' and whose Body.Status.Permissions contains PhysicalAccess.

steps.action: Submit the CSR to the bridge's pairing service and store the signed certificate, private key and bridge CA.
steps.expect: Signed client certificate returned in Body.SigningResult.Certificate (with Body.SigningResult.RootCertificate as the bridge CA); later LEAP connections on port 8081 authenticate with it.

request.service: LAP pairing (TLS-JSON on port 8083, not HTTP): Execute /pair with CommandType=CSR and Parameters {CSR, DisplayName, DeviceUID, Role}

steps.action: Reconnect on port 8081 with the new key, certificate and bridge CA and send ReadRequest /server/1/status/ping.
steps.expect: A ReadResponse whose Body.PingResponse.LEAPVersion names the bridge's LEAP version.

setup.notes: The Caseta bridge is Ethernet-only, so there is no WiFi provisioning. What does need documenting is the LEAP pairing handshake, because unlike most devices here the bridge issues the client a real X.509 certificate and refuses anonymous connections afterwards.

rejoin.notes: A router change is a cable move; issued client certificates survive. Clients must rediscover the bridge by TXT MACADDR, not by IP.

testing.notes: Probed live 2026-08-14 against the real bridge (same unit as the 2026-07-16 evidence; firmware has since moved 08.25.17f000 -> 08.28.11f000 per the _lutron._tcp CODEVER TXT). All four documented mDNS services re-observed (_leap 8081, _lap 8083, _lutron 22 with MACADDR/CODEVER/SYSTYPE=SmartBridge TXT, _hap 4548). The certificate-auth model was exercised to its gate: a TLS handshake on 8081 (LEAP) reaches the bridge's CertificateRequest (RSA/ECDSA client cert types listed) and is aborted by the bridge with a bad-certificate alert when no client certificate is presented; 8083 (LAP) behaves the same. Cross-check: the LEAP server certificate CN is SmartBridgeB894D9AABBCC — the MACADDR from the _lutron TXT record — and the LAP server cert chains to "Caseta Local Access Protocol Cert Authority". Halted at the physical pairing button (nobody home): CSR signing and authenticated LEAP commands remain unexercised by us.

entities.name: Caseta Dimmer
entities.notes: Unbound (identify_only): a dimmer is driven by a LEAP CreateRequest to /zone/{id}/commandprocessor with CommandType GoToDimmedLevel and DimmedLevelParameter {Level: 0-100} — Level 100 for on, 0 for off, the value in between for brightness. Documented for a future LEAP client; no declared command exists to bind.

entities.name: Caseta Switch
entities.notes: Unbound (identify_only): a switch is driven by a LEAP CreateRequest to /zone/{id}/commandprocessor with CommandType GoToSwitchedLevel and SwitchedLevelParameter {SwitchedLevel: On|Off}.

entities.name: Lutron Shade
entities.notes: Unbound (identify_only): a shade is driven by a LEAP CreateRequest to /zone/{id}/commandprocessor with CommandType GoToShadeLevel (open = level 100, closed = 0, position in between); tilt uses GoToTilt, and Raise/Lower/Stop exist for jog control.

enter.notes: Updates are started from the Lutron app and delivered through the vendor cloud. No LEAP command that starts or feeds an update is recorded, so a replacement client cannot update the bridge.

image.format: ZIP (stored) holding versionInfo, a sub-device firmware manifest, a SHA-256 manifest with a detached PKCS#7 signature, a per-package wrapped key + IV, and firmware.tar.enc (AES-128-CBC, OpenSSL salted format).
image.notes: Seven official "lite-heron" packages, 26.00.05f000 and 26.00.08f000-26.00.13f000, were fetched unauthenticated from https://firmware-downloads.iot.lutron.io/lite-heron/final/<version>/lutron_firmware (2026-08-15). 26.00.14f000-26.00.16f000 returned 404 on 2026-11-11, which does not prove nothing newer exists. The payload key is wrapped for the processor's own private key, which is not public, so no rootfs was decrypted. The package is signed; whether the bridge refuses an unsigned or altered one is not established. Whether these packages target this L-BDG2 at all is open: the probed unit reports CODEVER 08.x, and 08.x paths return 404.

dfu.notes: From the project's retained official packages and their analysis; nothing was installed. Do not install a package for research.

covers: Zone control, scenes, Pico button and occupancy events over LEAP (documented, not yet driven by this project).
Reading and editing the bridge's own timeclock schedules (see scheduling).
not_covered: Firmware updates, which go through the Lutron app and cloud.
Remote (off-LAN) access, voice assistants and the Lutron account.
Re-establishing trust after the client key is lost or a network reset drops issued certificates: that means pairing at the button again.
local_access.summary: LEAP is a cloud-independent local integration as shipped: pair once at the bridge button, keep the three resulting files (bridge CA, client certificate, client private key), and reuse them for every later LEAP session. No replacement cloud is needed. Pairing needs physical access; it is not a password reset or a way into somebody else's bridge.

events.notes: Button, zone and occupancy-group status arrive on subscriptions. Home Assistant exposes press, release and multi-tap for supported Picos on Caseta; LongHold is confirmed only on HomeWorks QSX, not Caseta. Older integration notes that say LEAP has no keypad events are out of date.

lap_pairing.notes: Port 8083 speaks LEAP-style JSON lines (not HTTP), but the pairing request names its operation in Header.RequestType ("Execute") rather than CommuniqueType. The TLS handshake needs a client certificate even here: open clients present a publicly distributed initial LAP certificate and key (not reproduced), and this project's 2026-08-14 probe saw the bridge abort a certificate-less handshake. The client then waits (pylutron-caseta: up to 180 s) for an unsolicited message whose Header.ContentType starts with "status;" and whose Body.Status.Permissions lists "PhysicalAccess" -- the button being held. Pairing is: Execute /pair with Body.CommandType=CSR and Parameters={CSR (PEM), DisplayName, DeviceUID, Role (Admin or Installer)}; a 200 reply carries Body.SigningResult.Certificate (the signed client cert) and Body.SigningResult.RootCertificate (the bridge CA to pin). Supporting exchanges: Read /certificate/root (fetch bridge root cert), Read /system/macaddress (stable identity), Execute /pair CommandType=Wipe (revoke certs; optional Filter.Subject.Organization), Subscribe /system/status/crosssign (cloud cross-sign progress). Responses carry an HTTP-style Header.StatusCode ("200 OK", "204 No Content", "401 Unauthorized") and the request's ClientTag. pylutron-caseta sends DeviceUID "000000000000" and Role "Admin". These management exchanges need the pairing channel; they are not an unauthenticated route to LEAP, and a network reset is not a shortcut around the button.

leap_protocol.message_envelope: Every LEAP frame is one JSON object: {"CommuniqueType": "...", "Header": {"Url": "...", "ClientTag": "..."}, "Body": {...}}. CommuniqueTypes seen in the app: CreateRequest/Response, ReadRequest/Response, UpdateRequest/Response, DeleteRequest/Response, SubscribeRequest/Response, UnsubscribeRequest/Response, MetadataRequest/ Response, ExceptionResponse. Each object is one line terminated by CRLF. Replies echo Header.ClientTag for correlation and carry an HTTP-style Header.StatusCode; large collections page with Header.Paging {Start, Count, Total}. Liveness check: ReadRequest to /server/1/status/ping (pylutron-caseta pings every 60 s with a 5 s timeout and reconnects on failure; the vendor app uses a 3 s timeout). A subscription returns current state and then events; after a reconnect, re-subscribe and re-read state. Subscriptions accept a ?where= filter, e.g. /zone/status/expanded?where=Level!:0 to list only zones that are on.

resources.notes: Read configuration dynamically; Caseta is device/zone based (RA3 and QSX use areas and /area/{id}/associatedzone instead). Zone commands go in Body.Command to /zone/{id}/commandprocessor; scenes are activated through the corresponding /virtualbutton/{id}/commandprocessor and Pico buttons through /button/{id}/commandprocessor. Further vendor-app CommandTypes beyond the entity notes: GoToShadeLevelWithTilt, GoToFanSpeed and GoToScene. No generic SetLevel exists. pylutron-caseta also reads /device/{id}/status for BatteryStatus.

leap_protocol.transport: Direct TLS socket with newline-delimited JSON; not ordinary HTTP or a required WebSocket handshake

remaining_unknowns: Whether port 8083 accepts a TLS client with no certificate while the button is held; open clients always present the initial LAP certificate, and this project only probed with the button released.
CSR signing, authenticated LEAP reads and every command remain unexercised by this project.
Whether this unit advertises SERNUM in its _lutron._tcp TXT; the probe did not record it.
Which firmware track the L-BDG2 is on: the probed unit reports 08.x CODEVER while the only public packages found are lite-heron 26.00.x.
Whether the bridge enforces the package signature, and its behaviour after an interrupted update.
Pico long-hold events on Caseta (LongHold is confirmed only on QSX) and which button events each Pico model emits.

scheduling.device_clock_dependency: The controller evaluates its own schedule and timezone. Local operation continues when the Internet is lost, but WAN-off firing and DST behavior still need validation for each controller.
limitations: LEAP and LIP integration IDs need not match; this Caseta non-Pro spec has no LIP fallback.
Scene, cover and button capabilities vary by controller. Do not invent a position for OpenCloseStop zones.
The vendor app's current enum uses GoToDimmedLevel/GoToSwitchedLevel; third-party GoToLevel is a compatibility command, not proof of a generic SetLevel API.
open_questions: Read-back of a newly created third-party event, WAN-off execution and DST/solar-offset behavior on this bridge.

event_model.AstronomicEventType: Optional solar event and signed offset
event_model.BeginDate: Start date for a dated rule
event_model.ScheduleType: DayOfWeek, ByDate, Daily or None in the current enum
event_model.exceptions: Recurring/nonrecurring execution and exception date lists

storage.notes: Use ByDate for a specific date. Do not assume every recovered schedule route exists on every processor.

scheduling.summary: LEAP timeclocks and their events are stored on the bridge and execute without the phone. Read /timeclock and /timeclock/{id}/timeclockevent; create, update and delete events with the corresponding CommuniqueTypes. Enable/disable through the event's status resource rather than deleting it, and test through the event's commandprocessor with TestThisTimeclockEvent.

steps.action: Read the controller's existing timeclocks and an app-created event before writing.
Create an event with CreateRequest /timeclock/{id}/timeclockevent and read back its assigned href.
Update only that event; enable it and the containing timeclock separately, then test it with TestThisTimeclockEvent.
